articles.title: Discussions on terrorism
articles.content: WHILE visiting the British parliament a few years ago, I was struck by the tradition —observed by prime ministers — of paying homage and expressing gratitude at the start of the weekly question time session to British armed forces personnel who had been killed or injured in action. It was the time of the Afghan war and British troops were stationed in Afghanistan. I thought it was a great tradition that reminded everyone of the sacrifices made by the soldiers and sent a powerful message to the troops that their countrymen had the highest regard for them and their sacrifices. Although Pakistan follows the British parliamentary system, almost all Pakistani prime ministers have avoided personally answering questions in parliament. As prime minister, Yousuf Raza Gilani used to answer many supplementary questions himself when he was in the House — but that was not a part of the set parliamentary procedure. Imran Khan had promised to follow this British tradition when he was prime minister and personally answer questions. However, he neither tried to change the parliamentary rules nor did he ever answer any questions in parliament. Both Houses and the provincial assemblies observe question hour but there is no parliamentary tradition of routinely acknowledging the sacrifices of the country’s shuhda and ghazis. The president, prime minister, ministers and senior civil and military officers do issue statements, and legislatures occasionally pass resolutions honouring those fighting a bloody war against terrorism; but the possibility of a weekly tribute did cross my mind. After all, hardly a day passes without hearing of security personnel — in the armed forces, paramilitaries, police and other security bodies — who have lost their lives in the line of duty. We need committees that are more active in debating national security. Almost all sources of information show that the number of violent terrorist incidents, casualties and fatalities in Pakistan have reached their highest level in a decade. In fact, 2025 was the bloodiest year since 2014. According to the South Asian Terrorism Portal, the number of violent terrorist incidents in 2025 was 1,077 with fatalities among the forces and civilians touching 1,229 and 655 respectively during the year. The data gathered for 2026 points to even higher figures when compared to the average monthly figures for 2025. For example, the number of terrorism incidents increased to a monthly average of 118, compared to 90 in 2025. Similarly, average monthly fatalities of civilian and security forces personnel in the first nine months of 2026 (up to Sept 21) have increased to 74 from 55 last year and to 114 from 102, respectively. These figures indicate a steep spike in attacks, particularly carried out by two major terrorist groups that the state aptly refers to asFitna al-KhawarijandFitna al-Hindustan. We do not see the level of concern and debate within democratic institutions that is warranted by the rise in acts of terrorism. We have four key standing committees relating to the issue in parliament — separate Senate and National Assembly standing committees on defence and two other committees of the Senate and National Assembly on the interior. In addition, each of the four provincial assemblies has a standing committee on home affairs. Whatever little record is available on these legislatures’ official websites does not indicate that the committees have been often and actively debating the rising incidence of terrorism in the country — especially in KP and Balochistan —in detail, which should have been done in view of the situation. The plenaries of the six national and provincial legislatures have debated the issue on and off, and passed resolutions too. I am sure that more frequent discussions in the legislative bodies would not only contribute to finding more effective ways in which the menace of terrorism can be combated at the people’s level, but the attention given by the legislators to this issue would further boost security personnel’s morale. In 2019, the Speaker of the National Assembly had constituted a joint (National Assembly and Senate) committee on national security under his own chairmanship and included the senior-most parliamentarians and ministers. But since thelast election in 2024,the committee has apparently ceased to exist. It doesn’t necessarily mean that we need a parliamentary committee on national security while the committees on defence and interior already exist. However, what we need are committees that are more active in debating national security. The public should be confident that national security issues are being discussed and timely decisions being made at the appropriate forum. In this context, it is difficult to understand the relatively inactive state of the National Security Committee, which was created in 2013. The Committee, which brings together the top civil and military leadership under the chairmanship of the prime minister, has not met even once during the current calendar year. Given the prevailing circumstances and the mandate of the NSC, it should meet more regularly, preferably on a monthly basis. Just for comparison, Britain’s National Security Council meets every week under the prime minister although the UK has far fewer security issues than Pakistan. It is hoped that the National Counter Terrorism Authority — a very important body especially in the present context — will not only become more active under its new national coordinator Maj-Gen Faisal Naseer but will also attempt to raise its public profile by, for example, sharing at least a sanitised version of the progress on the implementation of the National Action Plan with the people, their representatives and the media. Extending its outreach will bolster public trust. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.
articles.author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob

articles.title: The value of knowing
articles.content: WE are not short of information. We have never had more of it. Yet across the world, people struggle to answer the simplest questions: What actually happened? Who decided what? Is it true? This is the paradox of our age. The most connected societies in history are also among the most vulnerable to confusion, manipulation and distrust. Information moves faster than accountability. Algorithms reward outrage before accuracy. Artificial intelligence generates plausible falsehoods at scale. In such an environment, the right to know is not just a matter of transparency; it is the heartbeat of freedom. Without an accurate understanding of what is going on and what is being done in your name, the fog of deceit thickens, and bad actors can mislead with impunity. Society is most vulnerable when access to information is denied. Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition documented 313 internet shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025, the highest number ever recorded. Shutdowns block journalism, silence communities and deny people potentially life-saving information. Disinformation is not just a communications problem. It is a governance risk, an economic liability and a direct threat to people’s ability to make informed decisions. Access to information laws are an anchor of information integrity, and Unesco’s latest monitoring shows progress. Its 2025 survey showed that 141 countries have legal guarantees for access to information. But adoption is not implementation, and many countries still face practical gaps in oversight, appeals, enforcement, record-keeping and data management. Of the countries surveyed, 51 could not provide record-keeping data, despite reporting they had systems or procedures in place. Information commissioners and other overseers turn legal provisions into enforceable rights. Yet many of them are hampered by weak mandates, delayed appointments, budget cuts, political interference, limits on their powers and attacks on their independence. For access to information to work, these bodies must be protected by law, given adequate powers and resources, and shielded from undue influence. The gap was further confirmed by a 2025 test of access to information laws, jointly conducted by Unesco and the Centre for Law and Democracy. Across 146 identical requests in 76 countries, 38 per cent received no substantive response, only 42pc resulted in full disclosure, and the average response time was 22 days. A similar exercise will be repeated this year to measure any change. Access to information has to evolve, but examples of the shortcomings are everywhere, even in countries with well-intentioned legislation. And in an information vacuum, brave and independent journalism is indispensable. Journalism distils information into public understanding. It investigates, interrogates, corroborates and contextualises, but it also counters disinformation. It asks questions that some parties would rather avoid. And it gives citizens the means to participate meaningfully in public life. The damage caused by disinformation is real. Unesco estimates that individual disinformation cases can incur economic and social costs of $350 billion to $510bn, annually, through weakened public health responses, distorted elections, delayed climate action, financial losses, reputational harm and the erosion of trust in institutions. Disinformation is therefore not just a communications problem. It is a governance risk, an economic liability and a direct threat to people’s ability to make informed decisions. Public service broadcasters and independent news media organisations are a key counterweight to this problem. Their mandate is not to chase engagement at any cost, but to inform and serve all audiences. But they face the simultaneous pressures of fragmented audiences, declining trust, political interference, financial constraints, platform dependency and rampant false, synthetic and manipulated content. Their struggle to keep producing quality journalism is not a sectoral concern, it’s a democratic one. The response must include renewed investment in public-interest journalism, editorial independence, fact-checking, open-source verification, media and information literacy, and collaboration across borders. Just as falsehoods travel globally, so purveyors of trusted journalism must cooperate transnationally. The information ecosystem would be poorer and much more fragile without public service media — but they cannot defend it alone. On World News Day and the International Day for Universal Access to Information, the challenge is practical, and we call on all actors in the information space to do better: — Governments must enforce access to information laws and protect independent oversight. — Platforms and technology companies must take full responsibility for the information spaces they create, in total alignment with international human rights law. — And media organisations of all stripes should always choose rigour over reach. Free-flowing, reliable information is a shared benefit. But it depends on the authorities that protect access to information, journalists who pursue the truth above all else, and citizens’ right to the facts. The integrity dividend is real, but it is only paid when all of us play our part. David Walmsley is president, World Editors Forum, and editor in chief, Globe and Mail. Mariya Gabriel is assistant director-general for Communication and Information at Unesco. Liz Corbin is director of news, European Broadcasting Union. This opinion piece was commissioned to mark the International Day for Universal Access to Information and World News Day on Sept 28.
articles.author: David Walmsley | Liz Corbin | Mariya Gabriel

articles.title: Invisible risks
articles.content: ON the night of Feb 5, 2016, hackers pushed 35 fraudulent payment instructions through the SWIFT interbank messaging system. By the time Bangladesh Bank detected the breach, $81 million had left its account at the New York Federal Reserve and landed in the Philippines. Most of it was never recovered. There was no break-in, no border crossed, no vault touched — the heist happened entirely through a screen. But this is not only a story about central banks. The same battle is now fought daily on the phone in your pocket. It is the call from someone claiming to be ‘from your bank’, warning that your card is being blocked and asking you to ‘verify’ your details. It is the fake loan app, the link that looks exactly like your bank’s website but is not. The Bangladesh Bank robbers needed months of planning to trick a central bank. Today’s fraudster needs only a phone call and 30 seconds of your trust. The reason this matters to every Pakistani household is simple: our money now lives on digital rails. Nine in 10 retail payments in Pakistan are made digitally — the salary that arrives in an account, the pension drawn from an ATM, the remittance sent from Dubai, the utility bill paid from a mobile app, the shopkeeper’s QR code. In a single quarter, these transactions now approach Rs170 trillion in value. This is a genuine triumph of convenience and financial inclusion. But it also means that when the rails are attacked, it is not an ‘IT problem’ — it is your salary and your savings that are on the line. As mobile banking grows, so does the attack surface. And the attackers are getting smarter. AI, the same technology banks use to detect fraud, now helps criminals write flawless fake messages, clone voices and mimic official websites. Globally, nearly three in four people report that they, or someone close to them, were touched by cyber-enabled fraud last year. Pakistan is no exception: the credentials of more than 180m Pakistani internet users surfaced in a global data breach, and malicious software targeting banking apps on smartphones rose by more than half in a year. As mobile banking grows, so does the attack surface — and unlike a bank branch, a smartphone has no security guard. Banks themselves remain the most attractive target, for an obvious reason: they hold valuable information and they can move money. Global studies put the average cost of a single breach at around $5m — higher in finance — while institutions that invest ahead of the curve lose far less when trouble comes. The principle applies to a bank exactly as it applies to a household: prevention always costs less than loss. There is encouraging news. Pakistan has climbed from 79th to 29th on the ITU’s Global Cybersecurity Index in just three years. The State Bank has set up a dedicated Cyber Risk Management Department, launched Cyber Shield 2025-30, and this January conducted the country’s first industry-wide cybersecurity drill across 34 financial institutions — a recognition, at last, that an attack on one bank is a threat to all. Consider what disruption would actually feel like. If even a tenth of digital payments stopped for two days — apps down, cards declined, QR codes dead — transactions worth roughly Rs100 billion could be affected. The queue outside the ATM would be the least of it: shopkeepers unpaid, salaries delayed, and a corrosive question in people’s minds — is my money safe on this phone? That question, repeated often enough, would push people back towards cash and undo a decade of hard-won progress. Trust takes years to build and one bad weekend to lose. The task for Pakistan’s banks, therefore, is to move beyond minimum compliance towards genuine resilience. Cybersecurity must sit on the boardroom agenda alongside credit and liquidity risk — with continuous monitoring, tested defences, scrutiny of third-party vendors, and staff trained as rigorously as tellers once were trained to spot forged cheques. Banks, regulators and technology firms must also cooperate far more closely, because criminals collaborate freely while defenders too often work alone. The benchmark must be the attack withstood. But the reader has a role too, and it is decisive. Remember three things. Your bank will never — not once, not ever — call to ask for your PIN, password or the one-time code sent to your phone; anyone who does is a thief. A prize you never entered for is bait, and an offer too good to be true always is. And a moment’s pause before clicking a link is the cheapest security investment ever invented. The strongest firewall in the country is an alert customer. Bangladesh Bank lost $81m in a single night because attackers found an opening. The question — for every bank, and for every one of us holding a phone — is not whether such an opening exists. The question is whether we find it before they do.
articles.author: Zafar Masud

articles.title: India’s killer tourists
articles.content: THE date was January 2024, andIsrael’s destruction of Gazawas underway for all to see. Among the Israeli soldiers demolishing Palestinian homes was a man named Eitan Gilboa. In videos obtained by theHind Rajab Foundation, which analyses publicly available data to identify Israeli soldiers it alleges are implicated in war crimes, Gilboa and his unit can be seen detonating residential buildings and celebrating their destruction. The foundation alleges that in June of the same year, Gilboa was in Rafah ordering the demolition of multiple buildings and in July was involved in another demolition. It argues that Gilboa’s actions — and the actions of thousands of Israeli soldiers who took part in similar mayhem — are in violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention. Where do these Israeli war criminals go to ‘rest’ after destroying the lives of innocent Palestinians? Many go to India, following a backpacking route so well known for hosting Israeli soldiers that it is called the ‘Hummus Trail’. It stretches through destinations like Kasol and the Parvati Valley, Dharamkot and Tosh in Himachal Pradesh and on to places like Pushkar in Rajasthan, and Goa. Around 80,000 Israeli soldiers are said to travel there annually. This is also where Gilboa went. The path of guest houses frequented by Israeli travellers is well established and Indians have gone through a lot of trouble to accommodate them. Attractions include raves where visitors can lose themselves in trance music and drugs. So established is this trade in providing peace and ‘healing’ that one writer called towns on the Hummus Trail the “ashrams for war criminals”. Dharamsala even boasts of a ‘mini-Israel’, where shopkeepers speak Hebrew and serve Israeli food. In 2015, a cafe in Kasol was accused of refusing to serve Indian customers while admitting white tourists. Israeli soldiers reviled in other parts are welcome in India. The most important thing that India provides is absolution. Here, Israeli soldiers condemned and excoriated in most other parts of the world, are welcome. They can partake of a commercialised, tourist-friendly mix of ‘healing’ from the trauma of war, without having to take accountability for their actions in Gaza. Gilboa was no different. The Hind Rajab Foundation analysed photographs and other material from his Indian journey and filed complaints with the Himachal police, the home ministry and the Bureau of Immigration seeking his arrest. No arrest followed and Gilboa eventually left India. India’s ties with Israel run deep and increasingly point to an ideological, economic and military alignment. Hindutva’s founder Vinayak Damodar Savarkar praised the idea of a Jewish state in Palestine, describing Palestine as the Jews’ “Fatherland and Holyland”. Zionism’s blend of attachment to a motherland and religious attachment to a holy land was precisely what Savarkar wanted for Hindus. Modi’s India in this sense is like Zionist Israel. India’s Citizenship Amendment Act created an expedited route to citizenship for specified non-Muslim migrants from neighbouring countries while excluding Muslims from its provisions. Israel’s 2018 nation-state law similarly privileged Jewish national identity by declaring that the right to national self-determination in Israel is unique to the Jewish people. In contemporary India, the state supports these Israeli enclaves on the Hummus Trail even as it punishes people for expressing their support for Palestinians. An editorial published inThe Edict, a newspaper at Ashoka University, noted how eager Hindutva supporters want to fraternise with Israeli tourists, imagining their shared hostility towards Muslims as a natural alignment, while some Israeli travellers treat brown Indians as lesser locals there to serve them. In Pushkar,The Edictreported that the Chabad House has Hebrew signage and a perimeter fence, with Indians facing restrictions on entry while white tourists were admitted with less scrutiny. So India welcomes Israeli soldiers on their ‘healing journeys’, including those facing allegations of war crimes. The Indian state — as evidenced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s eager embrace of Israeli officials — is keen to emphasise the closeness of the two countries. In hisspeechat the Knesset, Modi even peddled yoga and ayurveda as sources of holistic wellness that Israelis could partake in when they visited India. This, then, is the tale of two hatreds. Men like Eitan Gilboa, accused of participating in the destruction of civilian homes, can leave Gaza and seek succour in a new environment where they can forget the cruelties of war. Hosting those accused of such acts without demanding accountability raises its own moral questions, but this is a truth that India, drowning in its own hatreds, appears unable to acknowledge. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: Gathering clouds
articles.content: THE clock may have been pushed back, but the countdown to another confrontation between the PTI and the state has not stopped yet. In one camp, a millennial politician is taking the big decisions, if only on behalf of a jailed Imran Khan. The chief minister of KP, Sohail Khan Afridi, is all of 37 years old. He wasslatedto lead the PTI this Sunday into yet another showdown with the state. Late Friday, however, his party’s long march to Islamabad was put off by a week, giving everyone some breathing space. Afridi must live up to some daunting expectations from the hardliners within his ranks. He has to succeed where others more experienced than him have failed, or face relegation and possibly political oblivion. The odds remain stacked against him, and the PTI’s opponents have left no stone unturned to impress upon him and his party what their prospects are if they march on Islamabad. That is why it would be premature to say the pressure has been released. Yet the other side is hardly in a better position. Intoxicated by the impunity granted to it under the current configuration of state, and seemingly oblivious to the optics and potential consequences of an overreaction on its part, the government is making it abundantly clear that it will ‘fix’ the PTI ‘for good’ if it dares march. That, however, will not solve its problems. Whatever calm the country has seen of late has merely been the lull before another storm. Ordinary Pakistanis have endured years of economic hardship. The protracted war in the Gulf has now handed this government another painful economic test — one it does not appear equipped to pass. Its show of strength is, in large part, a mask for that weakness. In short, both sides appear to be in varying states of desperation. And this is why the coming days could prove dangerous for the federation: a province marching on a barricaded capital. De-escalation is required, however remote a possibility it may seem at this point. Those in power must realise that no matter what they accomplish and no matter how comprehensively they are able to thwart the opposition, power is fleeting and the future will bring consequences in one form or another. Pakistan’s history is replete with missteps and unfortunate decisions that continue to hurt its present generations. The PTI, too, must realise that politics and negotiation remain the most viable path forward. There is a real danger that its march, if it goes ahead next weekend, may still end in violence and bloodshed. Fresh bloodshed will not advance its cause. Both sides must meet each other halfway, with the state permitting protest and the PTI keeping it peaceful, to prevent another tragedy from playing out.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Reducing the burden
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S students do not need voluminous textbooks especially in the early stages; they need better learning. The Punjab government’s decision to revise the curriculum from pre-primary to Grade 5, reduce textbook volume by 25pc, and shift students away from rote learning is therefore a welcome step. The current education system has confused the amount of content covered with learning. Crowded textbooks and examination practices have compelled children to memorise the text rather than understand the concepts, ask questions or apply knowledge. Reducing the syllabus can help correct this imbalance by giving teachers more time to explain and engage students. The proposed emphasis on learning outcomes is particularly important. Children should be able to demonstrate what they have understood, not simply reproduce what they have read. But this will require changes beyond the textbooks. Examinations must test comprehension, reasoning and application if schools are expected to teach those skills. This makes teacher training crucial to reform. Cambridge has been involved in reviewing the curriculum against international curricula and it is also expected to help train teachers. The government has proposed dedicating Saturdays to teacher training. These measures can work only if the training is practical and sustained. Yet another round of workshops and certificates will not change classroom behaviour. Teachers need support in lesson planning, assessment, classroom management and teaching children with different learning abilities. Moreover, teacher and student mental health counselling and a ban on corporal punishment will make schools safer, and replace fear and humiliation with healthier discipline. At the same time, the government should not overload the framework. AI education has merit, but primary schools must first secure reading, writing and maths. Implementation will determine whether the reform succeeds. Teachers should understand the purpose of the changes; textbooks must reflect them properly, and examinations should reinforce the new learning goals. The government will also need mechanisms to monitor classrooms rather than merely inspect whether new books have reached schools. The reduction in textbook volume is therefore useful, but it is not the reform’s most important feature. The significance of this step should lie in recognising that children learn better when education moves from content coverage to actual comprehension.
articles.author: Editorial
